rows.selection_reason: With no prior experiments, the most important task is to establish a reliable baseline that anchors all subsequent comparisons. config_001 (rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000) is the simplest configuration in the space: PCA is a deterministic, untrained dimensionality reduction (no encoder hyperparameters to confound interpretation), singleprofile avoids aggregation complexity, and RNA-only isolates one modality. This gives us a clean reference for RNA performance that every other RNA-based and multimodal configuration can be compared against. It is also computationally cheap, so if it underperforms we quickly learn that RNA alone is insufficient and can pivot toward image or multimodal settings with less wasted budget. Testing this first reduces the largest source of uncertainty—what the individual-modality floor looks like—before we invest experiments in more complex multimodal or learned-encoder configurations.

Evidence: Only one experiment is completed (config_001: RNA-only, singleprofile, PCA → 48.5% acc), which is near chance-level and tells us little about whether the image modality is informative or whether the low score is due to the encoder/modality choice. Uncertainty: The single most important open question for a multimodal study is whether the image channel carries complementary signal; without an image-only baseline, any future multimodal result cannot be decomposed into 'image contribution' vs. 'fusion synergy.' What this tests: config_010 (image_only, singleprofile, ResNet-50) is the cleanest single-axis comparison to config_001—same profile setting, same simplicity (no aggregation/fusion), but a different modality and a standard pretrained encoder. Why it is the best next experiment: It reduces the largest uncertainty (modality value) with a directly interpretable A/B comparison, establishes the image-only baseline needed to contextualize all subsequent multimodal runs, and uses a well-understood encoder (ResNet-50) so that any performance difference is attributable to the modality rather than encoder idiosyncrasy. Under a tight budget, knowing whether image features are useful at all before investing in fusion-strategy experiments is the highest-information-per-experiment choice.

Evidence: config_001 (RNA-only, pca_n2000, singleprofile) achieves 0.485 acc, while config_010 (image-only, resnet50, singleprofile) achieves only 0.208 acc, indicating RNA is the dominant signal and the image modality alone is weak. Key uncertainty: whether the image modality carries complementary information that, when fused with the strong RNA signal, yields a meaningful gain over RNA alone. This is the highest-impact strategic question because it determines whether the 36 multimodal configurations are worth exploring or whether budget should be spent entirely on RNA-side improvements. Config_016 (multimodal, singleprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, concat) is the cleanest test: it combines the exact components already validated in config_001 and config_010 with a simple concatenation fusion, isolating the effect of modality combination. If accuracy exceeds 0.485, multimodal fusion is validated and we can invest in optimizing it; if it does not, we can confidently rule out the resnet50-image branch and redirect budget to RNA encoder/profile improvements (e.g., multiprofile, scvi, scgpt). This single experiment resolves the most consequential design fork under the limited budget.

Evidence: config_016 (multimodal, PCA-2000 + ResNet50, concat) is the best result so far (Acc 0.527, F1 0.510), showing a ~4.2 pp gain over RNA-only (config_001, Acc 0.485) and confirming that fusion adds value despite the weak image-only baseline (config_010, Acc 0.208). Uncertainty: we have only tested one fusion strategy (concat); it is unclear whether weighted fusion would improve or degrade performance, and whether the fusion mechanism is a meaningful design axis worth further exploration. This experiment (config_017) is a clean single-variable ablation from config_016—changing only fusion from concat to weighted—so any performance difference can be attributed to the fusion strategy. Under a limited budget, this is the most informative next step: if weighted fusion helps, it validates a family of weighted configs (019, 021, etc.); if it does not, we can rule out fusion strategy as a key lever and redirect budget toward higher-impact dimensions (multiprofile, stronger encoders).

Evidence: The current best is config_016 (multimodal, single-profile, PCA_n2000+ResNet50, concat) at 0.527 acc, which beats RNA-only (0.485) by ~4 pts, confirming that fusion adds value. Concat and weighted fusion are nearly equivalent (0.527 vs 0.523), so fusion method is not the bottleneck. However, the profile-setting axis (single vs. multi) is completely untested, and it is a major structural design choice that could substantially change how much information the model extracts from the cellular data. Question: Does aggregating multiple cell profiles (via avgpool) on top of the already-validated PCA_n2000 + ResNet50 + concat pipeline yield a meaningful gain over the single-profile baseline? Why this is the best next experiment: config_018 is the minimal, most direct extension of the current best—changing only the profile setting to multiprofile with the simpler avgpool aggregation—while holding every other variable constant. This isolates the effect of multiprofile, making the result interpretable. If it improves, we have identified a new productive axis (and can then explore transformer aggregation); if it does not, we confirm single-profile sufficiency and can redirect budget toward the image-encoder or RNA-encoder axes. Under a tight budget, resolving this unexplored binary with a single clean comparison is the highest-information-per-experiment choice.

The strongest result so far is config_018 (multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, avgpool, concat) at 0.619 acc / 0.610 F1, showing that multiprofile + avgpool aggregation is the dominant performance driver. The single most important untested design question on top of this best config is whether the aggregation strategy can be improved: avgpool is a simple, unparameterized operation, while a transformer aggregation learns attention-weighted interactions across profiles. config_020 changes exactly one variable (avgpool → transformer) relative to config_018, making it a clean controlled test. In contrast, config_019 (weighted fusion) is expected to yield only a marginal difference based on the near-identical singleprofile results (0.527 vs 0.523). If transformer aggregation significantly outperforms avgpool, it identifies a high-value architectural direction; if it does not, we confirm that simple averaging is sufficient and can redirect effort toward RNA/image encoder upgrades. Under a limited budget, this experiment maximizes information gain about a key architectural choice while staying in the proven high-performing region.

Evidence: config_018 (multi-profile, PCA, ResNet50, avgpool, concat) is the clear best at 0.619 acc, and RNA is the dominant modality (0.485 alone vs 0.208 for image alone). However, all experiments so far use PCA—a simple linear dimensionality reduction—as the RNA encoder. The RNA encoder is the single most impactful untested design variable given RNA's dominance. Question: Does a learned, nonlinear RNA embedding (scvi_n200, designed for single-cell stochastic structure) outperform PCA in the best-performing multimodal multi-profile setup? Why this is the best next experiment: config_030 changes only the RNA encoder (PCA → scvi_n200) while holding all other settings at their empirically best values (multiprofile, avgpool, concat, ResNet50). This clean single-variable test directly quantifies the value of a learned RNA representation. If scvi improves substantially, it opens a high-value direction; if it does not, we can confidently rule out RNA encoder upgrades and pivot to the image encoder (ViT-L) as the next lever. No other untested configuration isolates as important an unexplored axis with as high expected information gain under the limited budget.

Evidence: The current best configuration is config_030 (scvi_n200, resnet50, avgpool, concat) at 0.632 acc / 0.607 F1. We have strong evidence that (a) multimodal > unimodal, (b) multiprofile + avgpool > singleprofile or transformer, and (c) scvi_n200 ≥ pca_n2000. However, the image encoder has only been tested as resnet50, which produced a very weak image-only baseline (0.208). The imagenet_vit_l encoder is completely untested and represents the largest remaining unexplored design axis. Question: Does upgrading the image encoder from resnet50 to imagenet_vit_l improve multimodal performance when paired with the best-known RNA encoder (scvi_n200) and aggregation (avgpool)? Why this is the best next experiment: config_036 isolates the image-encoder change while holding all other components at their empirically validated best values, directly extending the current champion. A positive result would identify a new promising direction and justify further exploration (weighted fusion, transformer aggregation with VIT-L); a null or negative result would efficiently rule out an entire family of 8+ configurations, saving budget. No other single experiment reduces as much uncertainty about a high-impact design choice.

The current best (config_036, 0.715 acc) uses scvi_n200 for RNA encoding. We have strong evidence that multiprofile + avgpool + concat + ViT-L is the optimal scaffolding, but we have zero data on scgpt as an RNA encoder. The two tested encoders (PCA, scvi) represent linear and VAE-based approaches; scgpt is a fundamentally different generative model that may capture cell-type structure better. Testing scgpt in the strongest known configuration (ViT-L, multiprofile, avgpool, concat) directly isolates the RNA encoder effect at the top of the performance range. If scgpt matches or exceeds scvi, it opens a new exploitation direction; if it lags, we can confidently rule out that branch and focus remaining budget on aggregation/fusion refinements. This is the highest-uncertainty, highest-potential-impact untested dimension in the search space.

The strongest evidence points to config_036 (scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + avgpool + concat, 0.715 acc) as the current best. The image encoder upgrade (resnet50→vit_l) yielded the largest single gain (~8%), and scvi+vit_l is clearly the dominant encoder pair. The remaining design uncertainty within this top region is the aggregation method: with resnet50, avgpool beat transformer by ~4% (0.619 vs 0.579), but that comparison was made with weaker image features. With the much richer vit_l representations, transformer aggregation could potentially capture more complex cross-profile interactions that simple averaging discards. config_038 is a clean single-variable change (avgpool→transformer) from the best config, directly testing whether the aggregation preference is robust across image encoder quality or whether the stronger features unlock a benefit for learned aggregation. If it matches or beats config_036, it opens config_039; if it underperforms, it confirms avgpool as the reliable choice and redirects budget toward other axes. This is the highest-information next step: it exploits the strongest direction while resolving a design choice that previously showed a meaningful performance gap.
